region: Pombo Rocks & nearby reefs, Tanzanian shore of Lake Malawi
description: A tiny but fiercely territorial mbuna banded in electric and navy blue, endemic to a short stretch of rocky Tanzanian shore. Best kept in large groups so aggression is diluted; long sold as Pseudotropheus demasoni.

region: Taiwan Reef, northern Lake Malawi (Malawi)
description: A small mbuna from a single reef with striking dichromatism: dominant males turn powder blue with black bars while females and juveniles stay bright yellow. Formerly Pseudotropheus saulosi; heavily exported and now bred widely in captivity.

region: Rocky shores of the Mozambique coast, Lake Malawi
description: A powder-blue mbuna whose dorsal fin carries a black submarginal band under a pale edge; both sexes look alike. One of the milder Pseudotropheus-type mbuna, and the source of the widely bred albino form.

region: Captive-bred
description: A line-bred albino of the powder-blue Pindani: pinkish-white with ruby eyes and only a ghost of the dark dorsal band. Same mild-for-an-mbuna temperament as the wild form.

region: Rocky shores of Lake Malawi
description: A slender, torpedo-shaped mbuna and one of the most belligerent of its group; dominant males are dark blue with black bars and fins. Many "elongatus" trade forms exist, some of which are separate species.

region: Lake Malawi — locality forms such as Ngara and Msuli
description: Unusual for an mbuna, acei forage in roving groups over sunken logs and reed stems, grazing aufwuchs from wood rather than rock. One of the most peaceful mbuna; the Msuli form has a violet-blue body and bright yellow fins.

region: Rocky reefs and caves throughout Lake Malawi
description: Juveniles and subordinate fish are yellow with dark bars, but dominant males can turn almost black within seconds. In the lake it picks parasites off the large catfish Bagrus meridionalis — and raids the catfish's eggs when it gets the chance.

region: Rocky coasts of Lake Malawi (widespread; many locality forms)
description: The classic barred zebra mbuna: males are sky-blue with bold black bars and a dark chin, grazing algae from rock faces and defending a cave. Females may be similar, brownish or orange-blotched (OB). Also sold as Metriaclima zebra.

region: Captive-bred (the OB pattern occurs naturally, mostly in females)
description: Orange-blotch zebra mbuna: a peach-orange body splashed with irregular black blotches. The OB pattern occurs naturally in several mbuna, mainly in females, and has been line-bred so that males show it too.

region: Mozambique shore of Lake Malawi (e.g. Minos Reef)
description: Despite the name, only females and juveniles are the classic orange-red; adult males are usually pale powder-blue with faint bars. A hardy, very common mbuna that grazes algae-covered rocks; also sold as Metriaclima estherae.

region: Mbenji Island, Lake Malawi
description: A case of reversed dichromatism: juveniles and females are pale blue with black bars, while mature males turn yellow-orange. Kenyi males are among the most aggressive mbuna and need a large, rocky tank with plenty of females.

region: Northern Lake Malawi, Malawi
description: A uniformly cobalt-blue zebra mbuna that lacks the bold bars of Maylandia zebra; whitish individuals are also sold. It grazes aufwuchs from shallow rock surfaces and is as territorial as its relatives.

region: Rocky shores of Lake Malawi
description: Males are pale ice-blue with a fiery orange-red dorsal fin and back, the combination behind the trade name "red top ice blue". Females are much duller, tan to brownish.

region: Tanzanian coast of Lake Malawi (Magunga, Lundo Island)
description: A strongly dichromatic, undescribed zebra-group mbuna: dominant males are blue-black with bright blue bars, while females and juveniles are vivid yellow-orange. Trade forms are named for their collection sites, e.g. "Msobo Magunga".

region: Likoma Island, Lake Malawi
description: A zebra-group mbuna from Likoma Island; males combine a golden-yellow body with a pale blue head and back crossed by faint bars, while females are drab yellowish-brown. One of the milder members of its genus.

region: Nakantenga Island, Lake Malawi
description: Named for its "fire back": males are sky-blue with black bars under a red-orange dorsal fin. A small zebra-group mbuna known only from the rocks around Nakantenga Island.

region: North-western Lake Malawi; the yellow form from Charo to Lion's Cove
description: One of the most peaceful mbuna: rather than grazing algae it picks insect larvae, snails and crustaceans from rocks and Vallisneria beds. Both sexes are lemon-yellow with a black band in the dorsal fin; males show more black in the pelvic and anal fins.

region: Hongi Island, Tanzanian coast of Lake Malawi
description: Males are pale blue with dark bars under an orange-red crown and dorsal fin; females are orange-brown. Like other Labidochromis it is a comparatively mild mbuna that picks small invertebrates and algae from the rocks.

region: Chizumulu Island, Lake Malawi
description: A small, slender Labidochromis from Chizumulu Island; both sexes are pale blue-white with dark vertical bars, males showing more blue and black in the fins. It picks tiny invertebrates from the rock surface with its pointed teeth.

region: Higga Reef, northern Lake Malawi
description: A pearly, almost white Labidochromis from Higga Reef whose German trade name means "mother-of-pearl". Peaceful for an mbuna, it feeds on tiny invertebrates picked from rocks.

region: Rocky shores of southern Lake Malawi
description: Females and juveniles are gold with two black, white-edged stripes; dominant males reverse the scheme to a near-black body with pale yellow stripes. Notoriously aggressive for its size and best kept with a single male.

region: Rocky shores of south-eastern Lake Malawi
description: Males are blue-black with electric-blue horizontal stripes, while females and juveniles are a uniform bright orange. Small but aggressive, it grazes aufwuchs and picks small invertebrates.

region: Maingano, Likoma Island, Lake Malawi
description: Both sexes are midnight-blue with two neon-blue horizontal stripes, making it one of the few mbuna without obvious dichromatism. Comparatively mild for its group; widely sold under the locality name "Maingano".

region: Chidunga Rocks near Chipoka, southern Lake Malawi
description: Often called the most aggressive of all mbuna: males are blue-black with pale blue stripes, while females are yellow with black stripes. Known in the wild only from the Chidunga Rocks off Chipoka.

region: Rocky shores of Lake Malawi
description: A slender Melanochromis whose females and juveniles are white with two black horizontal stripes; dominant males darken to a blue-black body with pale stripes. Quarrelsome like its relatives and needs plenty of rockwork.

region: Small islands of southern Lake Malawi
description: A rust-brown mbuna washed with lavender, both sexes alike; one of the gentlest mbuna and a good choice for mixed communities. It grazes aufwuchs from rocks in the shallows.

region: Rocky shores of Lake Malawi (many locality forms)
description: A zebra-like mbuna that hovers in open water above the rocks to snap up zooplankton, using the single-pointed teeth that set its genus apart. Males are blue with black bars and, in many forms, a yellow dorsal fin.

region: Gallireya Reef, Tanzanian coast of Lake Malawi
description: An undescribed Cynotilapia from Gallireya Reef whose males are bright blue with black bars and a red-orange dorsal fin; females are greyish. Like its relatives it feeds on zooplankton in the water column above the rocks.

region: Rocky shallows throughout Lake Malawi
description: A stocky algae-scraper with an overhanging snout and underslung mouth that lets it rasp aufwuchs while lying almost flat against the rock. Males are typically blue with faint bars; females range from brown to orange-blotched (OB).

region: Rocky shores of Lake Malawi (e.g. Thumbi West Island)
description: A slimmer cousin of Fuelleborn's cichlid with the same overhanging scraper snout; males of many forms are blue with a red-orange dorsal fin, females often orange-blotched. It grazes algae from steep rock faces, often hanging head-down.

region: Rocky shores of Lake Malawi
description: A large, deep-bodied mbuna whose broad mouth carries combs of tricuspid teeth for brushing loose algae from rock. Males are blue with dark bars and bold yellow egg spots; boisterous and best in a big rock-scape.

region: Rocky shores of southern Lake Malawi (many colour forms)
description: Recognised by its steep forehead and underslung mouth, used to comb algae and the small animals living in it from rocks. Males of most forms are dusky blue-grey with dark bars, while females are often golden yellow; long sold as Pseudotropheus tropheops.

region: Northern Lake Malawi, where rock meets sand
description: A mild mbuna that lives at the rock-sand transition, sifting sediment and picking food from the bottom rather than grazing rock faces. Males are pale blue with faint bars and dark pelvic fins.

region: Lake Malawi (several locality forms)
description: A cave-dwelling peacock whose males glow metallic blue with a yellow-orange wash on the lower flanks. Males hover near caves and hunt sand-dwelling invertebrates detected through enlarged sensory pores on the head.

region: Captive-bred
description: A line-bred peacock with a blood-red to orange body set off by a powder-blue face and dorsal fin, developed in captivity from Aulonocara jacobfreibergi. Females are a plain silvery brown.

region: Widespread in Lake Malawi (many locality forms, e.g. Ngara, Chilumba)
description: The most widespread peacock, with dozens of locality forms differing in how much yellow, orange or red marks the blue males. It hovers just above sand and hunts buried invertebrates by sensing them through enlarged head pores.

region: Maleri Islands, Lake Malawi
description: The "sunshine peacock": a natural stuartgranti form from the Maleri Islands whose males are bright yellow with a blue face and a pale-edged dorsal fin. Now mostly captive-bred.

region: Captive-bred
description: A man-made peacock line, generally traced to Aulonocara stuartgranti stock, in which both sexes are pinkish-white to orange speckled densely with red. Its exact parentage is debated and it has no wild counterpart.

region: Captive-bred
description: A man-made peacock carrying the orange-blotch (OB) pattern borrowed from mbuna, so males show patchy blue, orange and black over a pale body. It is a hybrid line with no wild counterpart.

region: Nkhomo Reef near Benga, central Lake Malawi
description: Males are canary-yellow with a blue face and faint blue bars, a combination that made it one of the most popular peacocks. It hunts invertebrates over sand near the rocky reefs of the Benga area.

region: South-eastern arm of Lake Malawi (e.g. Masinje, Makanjila)
description: Males are metallic blue with a bright red-orange patch on the shoulder just behind the gill cover, the mark behind its common name; females are brownish with dark bars. Like other peacocks it detects buried prey with the enlarged sensory pores on its head.

region: South-eastern arm of Lake Malawi
description: Males are deep blue with a brilliant sulphur-yellow to white blaze running from the snout over the head and along the dorsal fin. It lives around caves at the rock-sand interface, hunting small invertebrates.

region: Rocky reefs of Lake Malawi (Kadango, Mbenji and other forms)
description: A plankton-feeding "utaka" that hovers in loose groups above rocks; breeding males of the Kadango form have a blue head and a fiery red-orange body and fins. Females are silver with three dark spots.

region: Rocky reefs of Lake Malawi
description: Breeding males are an intense azure blue all over, with a white-edged dorsal fin and darker throat; females are silvery with dark spots. Like other utaka it feeds on zooplankton in open water near rocky reefs.

region: Lake Malawi (widespread)
description: Displaying males are blue-black on the lower body with a gleaming white-blue blaze along the back and dorsal fin; females are silver with three dark spots. A zooplankton feeder of open water near rocks.

region: Rocky habitats throughout Lake Malawi
description: Long sold as "Haplochromis ahli", males are vivid electric blue with darker bars, a white-edged dorsal and, in some forms, a red-orange anal fin; females are silvery-grey. In the lake it hunts juvenile mbuna among the rocks.

region: Lake Malawi; the Red Empress form from Namalenje Island
description: Breeding males of the "Red Empress" form have a turquoise-blue head and a body flushed red-orange with blue markings; females are silver with a dark horizontal stripe. In the lake it grazes aufwuchs and picks small invertebrates from rocks.

region: Sandy shallows throughout Lake Malawi
description: Named for its giraffe-like brown blotches on yellow, a pattern that lets it vanish against sand where it lies half-buried to ambush small fish. Breeding males develop a blue face and a golden-yellow body.

region: Sandy and weedy shallows throughout Lake Malawi
description: Famous for "playing dead": it lies on its side on the sand, its white-and-brown blotched pattern resembling a rotting fish, then snaps up small fish that come to scavenge. Breeding males gain a blue sheen over the blotches.

region: Rocky and vegetated shores throughout Lake Malawi
description: A heavily spotted ambush predator whose tan body is peppered with small dark-brown spots; breeding males develop a metallic blue head. It stalks small fish along rocky and weedy shores.

region: Rocky shores of Lake Malawi
description: Its long, down-angled snout lets it reach into rock crevices, where it ambushes small fish sheltering among the stones. The body is tan with large brown blotches; breeding males take on a blue sheen.

region: Vallisneria beds over sand, Lake Malawi
description: An extremely compressed, long-snouted ambush predator that hunts among Vallisneria, facing prey head-on so its razor-thin profile almost disappears. Despite the name it swallows small fish whole; males are metallic blue-green with a red-orange anal fin.

region: Sandy shores throughout Lake Malawi
description: A large sand-sifter that can dive in and bury itself completely when threatened. Females and juveniles are silver with rows of dark blotches; breeding males turn blue with a dark mask across the face.

region: Deeper sand-rock areas of Lake Malawi (e.g. Likoma Island)
description: A deeper-water hap that forages over sand and rock for small invertebrates, often in loose groups. Males are bright powder-blue with dark vertical bars, the first ones behind the head boldest; females are silvery-blue.

region: Tanzanian coast of Lake Malawi (e.g. Mdoka)
description: Named for its striking white lips, this hap lives over sand near rocks and feeds by sifting invertebrates from the bottom. Breeding males are deep blue with darker bars and a pale blue-white blaze along the back.

region: Rocky areas of Lake Malawi
description: Its enormous, fleshy lips are thought to help it suck invertebrates out of rock crevices, the same adaptation seen in Tanganyika's Lobochilotes. Males are blue with darker bars and pale lips.

region: Rocky shores of Lake Malawi (e.g. Zimbabwe Rock)
description: Males are blue-black with a vivid yellow blaze running from the forehead along the back and dorsal fin; females are silvery-grey with dark blotches. It forages for small invertebrates over rock and sand.

region: Rocky slopes of Lake Malawi
description: A large predator with a cavernous mouth that patrols rocky slopes for small fish. Females and juveniles are silvery with an oblique row of dark blotches from nape to tail; breeding males are flushed with blue and green.

region: Open water and rocky shores throughout Lake Malawi
description: A slender, fast-swimming hunter of open water that runs down small fish like a trout. Females and juveniles are silver with a dark horizontal stripe; breeding males turn metallic blue.

region: Sandy areas throughout Lake Malawi
description: Both sexes are pale sky-blue and grow a tall, dolphin-like nuchal hump with age. In the lake it shadows large sand-sifting cichlids to snap up the small animals they disturb.

region: Sandy and open-water areas of Lake Malawi
description: A big-mouthed hunter of small fish in open water over sand. Females and juveniles are silvery with a dark horizontal stripe, while breeding males become a bright yellow-green beneath a blue face.

region: Sandy and rocky shores of Lake Malawi
description: Named for the bold black band that runs obliquely from the nape to the base of the tail. Like other Mylochromis it uses strong pharyngeal teeth to crush snails; breeding males add a blue-green sheen.

region: Sandy bottoms of Lake Malawi
description: A sand-dwelling hap that takes mouthfuls of sand and sifts out insect larvae and other small invertebrates through its gills. Males are metallic blue with a yellow-orange margin to the dorsal fin; females are silvery.

region: Rocky shores of Lake Malawi
description: An unusual predator that often approaches small fish tilted on its side, its slim body and dark lateral stripe making it look like drifting debris until it strikes. Breeding males are suffused with metallic blue.

region: Rocky shores of northern Lake Tanganyika — Burundi, DR Congo & Tanzania
description: A graceful lyretail famous for cooperative breeding: older offspring stay in the territory and help guard younger broods, so a single pair can grow into a colony of dozens. Beige with white-edged fins and a black-and-yellow mark behind the eye.

region: Rocky shores of southern Lake Tanganyika — Zambia & Tanzania
description: A yellow-tinged relative of the Princess of Burundi and a model species in behavioural ecology: helpers in its family groups dig, defend and clean eggs in exchange for a place in the territory.

region: Rocky rubble zones of Lake Tanganyika
description: A slender, intensely lemon-to-orange cichlid that lives among rock rubble, picking small invertebrates from crevices. Pairs spawn hidden deep in caves and defend them vigorously.

region: Rocky shores of southern Lake Tanganyika (Tanzania)
description: A torpedo-shaped lamprologine banded with dark bars over a pale body, with electric-blue edges to the dorsal and anal fins. Pairs defend a cave fiercely and are among the more aggressive small Tanganyikans.

region: Rocky and shell-covered areas of Lake Tanganyika
description: Boldly marked with five black bars on a pale blue-white body and blue-edged fins, it closely resembles N. sexfasciatus. A robust snail-eater that crushes shells with strong jaws and defends its cave aggressively.

region: Rocky shores of southern Lake Tanganyika
description: Six bold black bars cross a body that is blue-white or, in the popular "Gold" forms, yellow, with blue-tinged fins. It feeds largely on snails crushed with stout jaws and is aggressive toward similar-looking fish.

region: Southern Lake Tanganyika (Zambia)
description: A small, peaceable lamprologine that nests in rubble or empty shells over sand; the dorsal fin has a bright yellow-orange edge and the tail is speckled with tiny dark dots. Pairs raise successive broods, tolerating older young in the territory.

region: Neothauma shell beds of Lake Tanganyika
description: Among the smallest of all cichlids: colonies live among beds of empty Neothauma snail shells, each fish guarding its own shells and constantly digging sand away around them. Females are noticeably smaller than males.

region: Neothauma shell beds of Lake Tanganyika
description: A colonial shell-dweller very like N. multifasciatus, but its dark bars continue over the head and onto the cheeks. Each fish guards a few empty snail shells within the colony.

region: Shell beds over sand, Lake Tanganyika
description: A tiny shell-dweller in which a male and female often share a single empty snail shell, retreating into it tail-first when alarmed. Pale beige with faint bars and a bluish sheen on the head.

region: Rocky shores of Lake Tanganyika
description: A member of the "princess" group of cooperatively breeding lyretails, set apart by its bright yellow head and throat. It lives in family groups among rocks, where older offspring help guard new broods.

region: Rocky rubble of Lake Tanganyika
description: A small member of the "princess" complex marked with dark bars on the rear body and a dark gill-cover spot. Like its relatives it lives in cooperative family groups among rock rubble.

region: Sandy and rocky shores throughout Lake Tanganyika
description: A robust predator of snails and small invertebrates that digs in sand to uncover prey. Silvery-grey with faint bars and rows of pearly spots; the dorsal fin carries a dark band under a white edge.

region: Caves and overhangs along rocky shores of Lake Tanganyika
description: A dark, elongate lamprologine that lives on the walls and ceilings of caves and overhangs, often hanging upside-down. The forked, lyre-like tail has elongated tips and the olive-brown body bears faint rows of pale spots.

region: Shell beds over sand throughout Lake Tanganyika
description: A pugnacious little shell-dweller that buries its snail shell in sand so only the opening shows, darting inside at any threat. Named for the dark, blue-bordered spot on its gill cover.

region: Captive-bred
description: A golden-yellow form of the shell-dwelling ocellatus, widely bred in the hobby. Behaviour is identical to the wild type: each fish buries and fiercely guards its own shell.

region: Shell beds and rocky areas of Lake Tanganyika
description: Shows the most extreme size difference between the sexes of any cichlid: territorial males, many times the weight of females, collect empty snail shells into a midden where the tiny females lay eggs inside the shells.

region: Shell beds of Lake Tanganyika
description: A small shell-dweller living alone or in loose groups among empty snail shells; its dorsal and tail fins are decorated with rows of fine dark lines, hence "ornate fin".

region: Rocky shores throughout Lake Tanganyika
description: One of the largest julies, yellow with four black horizontal stripes. Like all Julidochromis it hugs the rock face, often swimming sideways or upside-down along overhangs, and pairs spawn hidden in narrow crevices; the female is usually the larger partner.

region: Rocky shores of Lake Tanganyika
description: A small, golden-yellow julie with three black horizontal stripes, the most widely kept of its genus. Pairs claim a narrow rock crevice to spawn and raise successive broods there.

region: Rocky shores of Lake Tanganyika
description: A bold black-and-cream checkerboard pattern breaks up its outline against the rocks. A large, robust julie in which the female is often markedly bigger than the male and dominates the pair.

region: Rocky shores of north-western Lake Tanganyika
description: A small, dark julie whose black body is broken by rows of cream spots and a pale lower face, with blue-white fin edges. Secretive and rock-bound, it rarely strays from its crevice.

region: Rocky shores of south-western Lake Tanganyika
description: A brownish julie with three dark horizontal stripes and electric-blue edges to its dorsal, anal and tail fins. Like other julies it hugs the rock face and breeds in narrow crevices.

region: Rocky shores of Lake Tanganyika
description: A sleek, beige rock-dweller whose face is marked with bold black "bridle" lines; the fins are edged in blue-white. Pairs breed in caves and, like the related julies, stay close to the rock face.

region: Rocky shores of southern Lake Tanganyika — Zambia, DR Congo & Tanzania
description: Its razor-thin body lets it slip into narrow crevices to steal eggs and fry, while tough scales shield it from defending parents. Dark brown-black (pale in some forms) densely dotted with white; females are much smaller and spawn in holes or shells too tight for males.

region: Rocky shores of Lake Tanganyika
description: A deep-bodied, paper-thin egg-and-fry thief with a long, upturned mouth that probes rock crevices for shrimps and young fish. Colour varies by locality from red-brown to gold, crossed by dark bars.

region: Deeper rocky slopes of northern Lake Tanganyika (e.g. Burundi, Kigoma)
description: A slow-growing, deep-water cichlid with bold black bars on white-to-blue and a massive nuchal hump in big males. In the wild colonies hunt sleeping fish in the half-light of dawn; females mouthbrood a few large fry.

region: Deeper rocky slopes of southern Lake Tanganyika (e.g. Kapampa, Moba, Mpimbwe)
description: The southern counterpart of the frontosa, described in 2003; trade forms such as "Blue Zaire Kapampa" and "Mpimbwe" show intense blue on the face and fins. Like the frontosa it is a slow-growing mouthbrooder of deep rocky slopes.

region: Rocky shallows of southern Lake Tanganyika (dozens of colour races)
description: A rock-grazing herbivore found in dozens of geographic colour races; a classic pattern is a black body crossed by a broad red-orange band. Kept in large groups because males are intensely aggressive, and fed high-fibre, low-protein food to avoid bloat.

region: Kasanga, Tanzanian shore of southern Lake Tanganyika
description: The "red rainbow" moorii from Kasanga: an orange-red body shading to yellow-green on the head and gill area, one of the most colourful Tropheus races. Behaviour and care are those of the species.

region: Rocky shores of northern Lake Tanganyika (Tanzania & Burundi)
description: Juveniles are jet-black spangled with white spots, a pattern that fades with age into a dark body with a single broad white-to-yellow band and a blue face. It usually lives deeper than other Tropheus, grazing algae from rocks.

region: Rocky shallows of Lake Tanganyika (many local forms)
description: A variable Tropheus whose young are dark with pale vertical bars; adults of many races are olive-brown with yellowish bars or flushes. Like all Tropheus it lives in the surge zone, grazing aufwuchs from rock.

region: Open water over rocky slopes, Lake Tanganyika (forms e.g. Utinta, Kitumba)
description: A slender planktivore that forms huge shoals in open water over rocky slopes; males flash yellow or blue tails depending on population. Unusually, spawning takes place in mid-water, the female catching the eggs before they sink.

region: Caves and rock overhangs of Lake Tanganyika
description: A slender, dusky-violet planktivore with neon-blue horizontal lines that hangs in loose groups beneath overhangs and in caves, often aligned with the rock ceiling. Females mouthbrood a few large fry.

region: Sandy shores of Lake Tanganyika
description: A sand-dwelling cichlid that forms monogamous pairs in which both parents take turns mouthbrooding the eggs and fry, a rare arrangement among cichlids. Pale sandy body with a bright yellow dorsal fin.

region: Rocky shores of southern Lake Tanganyika
description: Unlike most of its sand-dwelling genus, papilio lives among rocks; its tall dorsal fin flashes yellow and blue like a butterfly wing. Pairs share mouthbrooding of the small broods.

region: Sandy shores of Lake Tanganyika
description: A pale sand-dweller that forages in loose groups, sifting mouthfuls of sand for small invertebrates. Breeding males show the yellow cheeks behind its name and a scatter of fine iridescent spots.

region: Sandy shores of Lake Tanganyika (e.g. Kilesa)
description: A schooling sand-sifter; breeding males transform into shimmering silver-blue fish with iridescent lines and a black throat, displaying over small sand craters in leks. Long sold as Xenotilapia melanogenys.

region: Rocky shores of southern Lake Tanganyika
description: Males are velvety blue-black with long pelvic fins tipped by yellow-orange lappets that mimic eggs; during spawning the female nibbles at them and takes in sperm. Males defend spawning sites on rock surfaces.

region: Rocky shallows of south-eastern Lake Tanganyika
description: Its large eyes give it the name boops ("ox-eyed"); males are dark iridescent blue-black with a pale-edged dorsal fin and long egg-dummy pelvic fins. Males defend rock-top spawning sites in shallow rocky habitats.

region: Rocky shores of Lake Tanganyika
description: Mature males develop a fleshy, bulbous nose overhanging the mouth along with long yellow-tipped pelvic fins; some populations have a pale or yellow blaze. Females are silvery.

region: Rocky and sandy shores throughout Lake Tanganyika
description: Males shimmer metallic blue, green or purple and trail extraordinarily long yellow-tipped pelvic fins; each builds a sand crater on top of a rock and displays above it to passing females. Females are silvery.

region: Sandy-rocky shores of Lake Tanganyika
description: Males build sand bowers and are yellow with fine iridescent blue horizontal lines along the flanks; females are silvery-brown. It feeds on small invertebrates picked from sand and rock.

region: Sandy shallows throughout Lake Tanganyika
description: A sand-sifter of shallow beaches; breeding males glow salmon-pink with rows of iridescent red and blue spots and dig crater nests in the sand. Females are silvery-beige.

region: Sandy shallows of Lake Tanganyika
description: The smallest Callochromis, a sand-dweller whose males are spangled with iridescent blue and orange-red spots, on a bright yellow-orange ground in some populations. It sifts sand for invertebrates and spawns in shallow pits.

region: Wave-washed rocky shallows of Lake Tanganyika
description: A "goby cichlid" of the surf zone with a reduced swim bladder, so it hops from rock to rock rather than swimming, scraping algae with spatula-shaped teeth. Pairs share mouthbrooding: the female carries the eggs first, then passes them to the male.

region: Wave-washed rocky shallows of Lake Tanganyika
description: A stocky goby cichlid of the surf zone, olive-brown sprinkled with bright blue spots, that hops over rocks grazing algae. Like its relatives it has a reduced swim bladder, and pairs share mouthbrooding duties.

region: Shallow rocky shores of northern Lake Tanganyika
description: The smallest goby cichlid, yellowish-olive with dark bars and golden spots and pale stripes across the head. It hops along shallow, wave-washed rocks picking tiny invertebrates from the algae; pairs share mouthbrooding.

region: Rocky and shell-strewn shores of Lake Tanganyika
description: A small, slender, pale cichlid with a bold dark horizontal stripe that lives among rocks and empty snail shells. Pairs spawn in narrow crevices or shells and defend them stubbornly.

region: Rocky shores throughout Lake Tanganyika
description: A sturdy, brown-olive cave-spawner of rocky shores with a dark stripe behind the eye; unusually, some populations include a dwarf morph that breeds inside empty snail shells.

region: Rocky shores of southern Lake Tanganyika
description: Juveniles are bright yellow, but adults turn a velvety jet-black. Unusually for a lamprologine it lays its eggs in the open on rock and grazes aufwuchs; pairs are fiercely territorial.

region: Rocky shallows of southern Lake Tanganyika
description: A large algae-grazer that combs aufwuchs from rock with rows of tiny teeth; dark brown-black covered in pale spots, with long trailing tips to the tail fin. Very aggressive, kept in large groups in big tanks.

region: Shallow rocky shores of Lake Tanganyika
description: A small algae-scraper of shallow rocky shores whose males carry long pelvic fins and, in many populations, a golden-yellow head and flanks. A maternal mouthbrooder, relatively mild for a Tanganyikan grazer.

region: Rocky shores and shell beds of southern Lake Tanganyika
description: A slender, predatory lamprologine with rows of dark spots on a silvery-gold body that hunts small fish around rocks and shell beds. Pairs breed in caves and guard large broods.

region: Rocky shores of Lake Tanganyika
description: An elongate ambush predator of rocky shores, mottled brown with dark bars and blotches that blend into the rocks. Large pairs guard their cave and fry aggressively.

region: Rocky slopes throughout Lake Tanganyika
description: One of the largest lamprologines, a slender piscivore with very small scales, dark bars on a pale body and white-edged fins. It hunts small fish along rocky slopes and is very aggressive when breeding.

region: Deep water (below ~30 m) along rocky slopes of Lake Tanganyika
description: A deep-water planktivore that lives in schools well below the depth most divers reach; males develop a pink-purple sheen, a bluish face and long pelvic fins. Females mouthbrood the young.

region: Shallow rocky shores throughout Lake Tanganyika
description: A stocky, thick-lipped algae-grazer of shallow rocky shores, olive-green with rows of dark spots along the flanks. Aggressive toward its own kind; females mouthbrood the fry.

region: Rocky shores throughout Lake Tanganyika
description: Its huge, fleshy lips seal against rock while it sucks crabs, insect larvae and other invertebrates out of crevices. Silvery-yellow with dark bars; a large, robust species for big tanks.

region: Open water and shores throughout Lake Tanganyika
description: The largest cichlid in the world, reaching about 80 cm in the lake, with tiny scales and a silvery body. Pairs guard their huge broods for months; in captivity it is kept only by public aquaria.

region: Rocky and rubble shores throughout Lake Tanganyika
description: A tan cichlid with dark vertical bars and a highly protrusible mouth that it shoots forward to pick small invertebrates from rock and sand. Lives in loose groups over rubble; females mouthbrood the fry.

region: Rocky islands of southern Lake Victoria, Tanzania
description: A textbook case of speciation by sexual selection: males are crimson along the back over yellow flanks with black bars, and females of each island population prefer their local male colours. Females are drab yellow-brown.

region: Rocky shores of Lake Victoria (Tanzania, Kenya & Uganda)
description: Males are metallic blue-grey with bold black bars and reddish fin edges; it coexists at many islands with the red-backed P. nyererei, the two kept apart mainly by female colour preference. Females are yellowish-brown.

region: Lake Victoria basin (Uganda)
description: An undescribed Victorian haplochromine whose males have a blue body with black bars under a fiery orange-red back and dorsal fin. Like many Lake Victoria cichlids it now survives in the hobby mainly through captive breeding.

region: Lake Kyoga system, Uganda (Lake Victoria basin)
description: Males are golden-yellow with broad black bars and red on the throat, belly and fins, earning the trade name "zebra obliquidens". Native to the Lake Kyoga system, where it has become rare, it is now widely captive-bred.

region: Shores of Lake Tanganyika and its inflowing rivers & swamps
description: A model animal in neuroscience: when a male rises to dominance he turns bright yellow or blue with a black eye bar and red shoulder patch within minutes, while his brain and hormones reorganise. Spawning females nip at the egg spots on the male's anal fin.

region: Lake Victoria; now mainly in captivity
description: A plant- and algae-eating Victorian haplochromine; males combine a red lower body and fins with a green-blue back and dark bars, the colours behind its trade name. Like many Lake Victoria cichlids it declined sharply after the Nile perch was introduced.

region: Coastal southern Nigeria and western Cameroon; soft to slightly brackish waters
description: The classic West African dwarf cichlid: pairs claim a cave and the female, her belly glowing cherry-red, courts the male with curved-body displays. Both parents escort clouds of fry around the tank.

region: Captive-bred
description: A widely bred albino kribensis: creamy-white with ruby eyes, a pink belly and yellow-edged fins, but with the same cave-spawning, fry-herding behaviour as the wild form.

region: Coastal forest streams of Nigeria and Cameroon (many locality forms)
description: A smaller, more delicate krib from soft, acidic forest streams, traded in many locality forms that differ in belly, gill and fin colours. Males have spotted, striped tail fins; breeding females show a glowing, often violet-tinged belly.

region: Coastal Gabon to the lower Congo, often near estuaries
description: A coastal krib that tolerates slightly brackish water; breeding females darken dramatically, showing a pale band and a pinkish-violet belly. Males carry a dark spot at the rear of the dorsal fin.

region: Rivers and swamps of West Africa
description: A brilliant red cichlid spangled with turquoise sequins and marked by a dark mid-body spot; pairs are devoted parents but very aggressive while breeding. Many "jewel cichlids" in the trade are actually related species such as H. guttatus.

region: Congo River basin (Ubangi drainage) — DR Congo & Central African Republic
description: A smaller, deeper-red jewel cichlid from the Congo basin, glowing blood-red with rows of blue sequins; its dark spots are faint or absent. Somewhat milder than its West African relatives, it guards its fry as a pair.

region: Rivers, lagoons and lakes of West and Central Africa, Senegal to Congo
description: A large, predatory jewel cichlid, olive-yellow with five big black blotches along the flank and a red flush when breeding. It hunts small fish in rivers and lagoons and is very aggressive.

region: Coastal streams of Sierra Leone, Guinea and Liberia
description: A small, peaceful West African cichlid whose pearly body is crossed by dark bars and sprinkled with iridescent blue spots. Pairs spawn on flat stones or leaves and lead their fry around in a tight cloud.

region: Lake Mai-Ndombe, DR Congo
description: Named because the female is the gaudier sex: she sports a pink-red belly and a white-banded dorsal fin, while the male is grey with fine dark lines. It comes from the very soft, acidic black water of Lake Mai-Ndombe.

region: Lower Congo River (Malebo Pool region)
description: A slender, flat-bellied dwarf cichlid of the Congo rapids that keeps close to the bottom among rocks; its body has a bluish-violet sheen and breeding females a swollen violet belly. Pairs spawn in caves and defend them doggedly.

region: Rapids of the lower Congo River
description: A rapids-dweller with a reduced swim bladder that hops along the bottom; mature males grow a large fatty hump on the forehead. Pairs dig caves under rocks and stay together long-term.

region: Rapids of the lower Congo River
description: A very slender, elongate rapids cichlid that rests and hops on the bottom among stones of the lower Congo; mature males develop a modest forehead hump. Pairs breed in caves dug beneath rocks.

region: Coastal swamps and forest streams of West Africa (Ivory Coast to Nigeria)
description: A shy cave-spawning cichlid of slow-flowing coastal swamps and forest streams, olive-brown with dark spotting and a dark eye-spot in the soft dorsal fin. Pairs guard their fry among roots and leaf litter.

region: Coastal rivers of Guinea-Bissau, Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia
description: Bold black bars on a cream-to-yellow body give it the "hornet" name; one of the most aggressive cichlids in the hobby, it digs constantly and uproots plants. Long sold as Tilapia buttikoferi.

region: Coastal rivers and lagoons of West Africa (Ivory Coast to Cameroon)
description: Juveniles are boldly barred, while adults turn olive-gold with a row of large black blotches along the flank. Pairs spawn on hard surfaces and guard their fry; introduced populations have become invasive in Florida and elsewhere.

region: Coastal rivers of West Africa, Sierra Leone to Cameroon
description: Eggs are laid on a carefully cleaned stone, but once fertilised the male — sometimes helped by the female — takes them into his mouth to brood. Golden-olive with faint bars and a dark spot in the dorsal fin; it sifts sand for food.

region: Rapids of the lower Congo River
description: A worm-like, elongate rapids cichlid that lives in crevices between stones in strong current, its swim bladder reduced. Females are smaller and show white-edged fins with a pinkish band; pairs are intolerant outside spawning.

region: Lake Tseny area, north-western Madagascar
description: A deep-bodied, silvery-pink Madagascan cichlid marked with fine dark pinstripes along its scale rows. Nearly lost in the wild, it survives largely thanks to captive-breeding programmes in zoos and among dedicated hobbyists.

region: Lakes of north-western Madagascar
description: A deep-bodied, silvery-grey Madagascan cichlid marked with dark blotches on the flank, from a handful of lakes in the north-west. Critically endangered by habitat loss and introduced fish, it is maintained in zoo and private breeding programmes.

region: Rivers, lakes and brackish lagoons of eastern Madagascar
description: The only widespread Paretroplus of Madagascar's east coast, living in rivers, lakes and brackish lagoons. Deep-bodied and dusky grey-brown with darker bars; a large, robust species for big tanks.

region: Nosy Be and the Sambirano region, north-western Madagascar
description: A sturdy, deep-bodied cichlid of north-western Madagascar, olive to yellowish with a series of dark vertical bars. Pairs spawn on cleaned rock and guard eggs and fry together.

region: Coastal rivers and lagoons of eastern Madagascar
description: A robust Ptychochromis of Madagascar's eastern coastal waters that tolerates brackish lagoons. Olive-grey with dark bars; pairs defend a territory and raise their fry together.

region: Mangarahara River, northern Madagascar
description: Feared extinct after its only river was dammed and dried, a few surviving fish were located in 2013 and became the founders of a captive-breeding programme. A deep-bodied, dark-barred substrate-spawner.

region: Rivers and lakes across Madagascar
description: A black cichlid spangled with iridescent blue-white spots, among the most widespread native fishes of Madagascar. Pairs spawn on hard surfaces and guard their fry; it is now pressured by introduced species.

region: Coastal lagoons, estuaries and rivers of southern India and Sri Lanka
description: Known as karimeen in Kerala, where it is a prized food fish, this deep-bodied cichlid lives mainly in brackish lagoons and estuaries. Greenish-grey with dark bars and rows of pearly spots; pairs guard eggs attached to submerged surfaces.

region: Fresh and brackish coastal waters of southern India and Sri Lanka
description: A small, golden-orange cichlid with rows of red spots and a large black blotch mid-flank, often sharing lagoons with the green chromide. Pairs spawn on a cleaned stone, and the young feed partly on mucus "glanced" from their parents' skin. Formerly Etroplus maculatus.

region: Mozambique shore of Lake Malawi; mostly captive-bred
description: An orange-blotched (OB) red zebra: a peach-orange body splashed with irregular black blotches. OB individuals occur naturally among red zebra females and are line-bred in the hobby.

region: Nkhata Bay area, north-western Lake Malawi
description: The pale bluish-white form of Labidochromis caeruleus, closer to the colour the species was named for than the familiar yellow lab, with the same black band in the dorsal fin. Like the yellow form it picks invertebrates from rocks and plant beds.

region: Coastal rivers of West Africa (Ghana to Cameroon)
description: Much of the "jewel cichlid" stock in the trade belongs to this species: brick-red to scarlet with glittering blue spots, a dark spot on the gill cover and another mid-flank. Pairs dig pits, spawn on stones and are ferocious in defence of their fry.
